meta_desc: A clear NCERT Class 5 Maths Can You See the Pattern? study guide with number, tile and magic-square rules, solved case studies and a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: NCERT Chapter 7 looks like a page of pretty borders and squares, but every pattern hides a rule you can write down. Here is how I teach Class 5 to find the rule, with two solved case studies and a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Draw the number 3 on a page, then its mirror image beside it, and a ten-year-old will grin before you say a word. That small delight is the whole point of Class 5 Maths Can You See the Pattern? — NCERT Chapter 7. It is one of the few chapters where a child sees a rangoli border, a bathroom tile, or a magic square and slowly realises there is a rule hiding underneath. The chapter is not asking students to memorise sums. It is asking one question, over and over: what is the rule, and can you use it to predict what comes next?

I have taught this chapter to plenty of Class 5 groups, and the ones who struggle are almost always the ones hunting for a formula. There isn’t one. The skill is spotting the rule yourself. Below I break the chapter into its three real ideas, then work through two case studies of the kind you meet in exams.

What Can You See the Pattern? actually covers

The NCERT chapter blends three families of pattern that feel different but reward the same habit of mind.

  • Shape and motif patterns — a single figure that rotates or flips step by step to build a border, and tile patterns that repeat to cover a floor.
  • Number patterns and number rules — growing sequences, and those satisfying ‘calculator surprise’ rules like 1 × 8 + 1 = 9, 12 × 8 + 2 = 98, and so on.
  • Magic squares — grids where every row, column and diagonal add to the same total.

Rotating and repeating motifs

A border pattern usually takes one motif and turns it a quarter-turn (90 degrees) each step, so the shape faces up, then right, then down, then left, and repeats. Tell your child to track a single corner or a single dot through the turns rather than the whole shape at once. A tile pattern is gentler: the same tile repeats without turning, and the puzzle is which tile fills the gap so the joins still line up.

Number rules you can write down

The number-rule pages look like magic, and children love them, but the honest lesson is that each one is a rule in disguise. Take the staircase: 1, 121, 12321, 1234321… produced by squaring 1, 11, 111, 1111. Once a child sees why the digits climb and fall, the pattern stops being a trick and becomes something they can extend to the next line themselves.

The one habit that cracks every pattern

Whatever the pattern, the method is the same three steps, and I make students say them out loud.

StepWhat to doExample on 2, 4, 8, 16…
1. CompareLook at how each term relates to the one beforeEach number is the previous one doubled
2. State the ruleSay the rule in one plain sentence‘Multiply by 2 each time’
3. PredictUse the rule to find the next term, then check16 × 2 = 32, so the next term is 32

The predict-then-check step is the one most children skip, and it is the one that matters. Guessing the next shape is a party trick. Stating a rule and testing it is mathematics. Here is a small caveat worth passing on: some sequences fit more than one rule for the first few terms, so a good answer names the rule, it does not just extend the list.

Case study 1: The rangoli border

This is the passage-style question the case-study booklet is built around, so it is worth walking through slowly.

Meera is drawing a rangoli border for Diwali. Her motif is a single leaf pointing up. In the next box the leaf points right, then down, then left, then up again, and the four-step cycle repeats along the whole border.

  • Which way does the leaf point in the 7th box? The cycle is 4 boxes long (up, right, down, left). Box 5 restarts at up, box 6 is right, box 7 is down. So the leaf in the 7th box points down.
  • How many complete cycles are there in 20 boxes? 20 ÷ 4 = 5, so there are exactly 5 complete cycles with none left over.
  • Which boxes show the leaf pointing left? Left is the 4th position in each cycle, so boxes 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 — every multiple of 4.

Notice what did the heavy lifting: the number 4. A rotating border is really a counting-in-4s problem wearing a costume. Once a child spots that, ‘the 50th box’ is no harder than the 7th — 50 ÷ 4 leaves remainder 2, so it matches box 2, pointing right.

Case study 2: The magic square

Ravi fills a 3-by-3 grid with the numbers 1 to 9 so that every row, column and diagonal adds to the same total. He has placed 8, 1 and 6 across the top row, and 5 in the very centre.

  • What is the magic total? The top row is 8 + 1 + 6 = 15, so every line must total 15.
  • What goes in the bottom-right corner? The diagonal from top-left runs 8, 5, and the corner. 8 + 5 = 13, and 15 − 13 = 2, so the bottom-right corner is 2.
  • Why is 5 always in the centre? The centre lies on 4 different lines, so it must be the middle value of 1 to 9. That is 5. This is the counter-intuitive gem of the whole chapter: the centre of a 3-by-3 magic square is fixed before you place anything else.

When I show a class that last point, someone always tries to prove me wrong by putting a different number in the middle — and it never balances. That failed attempt teaches more than a worked answer ever could.

Common slips to watch for

Two mistakes come up again and again in Class 5 Maths Can You See the Pattern? work. First, children track the whole rotating shape instead of one fixed point, and lose the direction by the third turn. Second, in magic squares they check rows and columns but forget the two diagonals, so a ‘finished’ square that fails a diagonal slips through. A thirty-second diagonal check at the end catches it every time.

quiz.title: Class 5 Can You See the Pattern? Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on rotating motifs, number rules and magic squares from NCERT Chapter 7. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 7, Can You See the Pattern?

questions.q: In the pattern 3, 6, 12, 24, what is the rule?
questions.explanation: 3 to 6, 6 to 12 and 12 to 24 all double, so the rule is multiply by 2 each time.

questions.q: A leaf motif turns a quarter-turn each box: up, right, down, left, then repeats. Which way does it point in the 6th box?
questions.explanation: The cycle of 4 restarts at box 5 (up), so box 6 is right.

questions.q: In a border with a 4-step cycle, which boxes show the last position of the cycle?
questions.explanation: The 4th position lands on boxes 4, 8, 12, 16 and so on, that is every multiple of 4.

questions.q: The top row of a 3-by-3 magic square is 8, 1, 6. What must every row, column and diagonal add to?
In a magic square using 1 to 9 with total 15, which number always sits in the centre?
questions.explanation: The centre lies on four lines, so it must be the middle value of 1 to 9, which is 5.

questions.q: Following the rule 1, 121, 12321, what comes next?
questions.explanation: These are the squares of 1, 11, 111, then 1111, which gives 1234321.

questions.q: A tile pattern repeats the same tile without turning it. What decides the correct missing tile?
options: That it is the biggest tile
That the joins still line up
questions.explanation: A repeating tile must keep the edges and joins lining up with its neighbours.

questions.q: In a border with a 4-step cycle, which box matches the same position as the 2nd box?
questions.explanation: Positions repeat every 4 boxes, so box 6 (6 minus 4 = 2) matches the 2nd box.

faq.q: What is NCERT Class 5 Maths Chapter 7 about?
faq.a: Chapter 7, Can You See the Pattern?, teaches students to find the rule behind number sequences, rotating and repeating shape patterns like borders and tiles, and magic squares where every row, column and diagonal share the same total.

faq.q: How do you solve a rotating border pattern?
faq.a: Track one fixed point of the motif, not the whole shape, and count the length of the repeating cycle. If the cycle is 4 boxes long, divide the box number by 4 and the remainder tells you which position it matches.

faq.q: Why is 5 always in the centre of a 3-by-3 magic square?
faq.a: The centre cell sits on four different lines, so it has to be the middle value of the numbers 1 to 9. That middle value is 5, which is why every standard 3-by-3 magic square puts 5 in the centre.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake in this chapter?
faq.a: Forgetting to check the two diagonals in a magic square, and losing track of direction in a rotating pattern by following the whole shape instead of one corner or dot. A quick diagonal check at the end fixes the first.
